title: Joy to wrestle (Tanya 26)
hookLine: a sluggish wrestler can't win; sadness weighs down service
tomorrow: a verse says the wicked just vanishes. why did a rebbe hear hope?

lines: THIRD PERIOD. THE BIG KID IS LOSING.
A BEAT LATE ON EVERY MOVE.
WHO WINS WHEN STRENGTH SHOWS UP HEAVY?
cards: Third period of a high school wrestling match, and the bigger kid is losing. He should win. He's stronger, heavier, been on the mat longer.
But he's been off since the whistle: shoulders down, a beat late on every move. The smaller kid isn't stronger. He's just quick, and he looks like he's having fun out there.
Coaches have a word for what's wrong with the bigger kid. So does a book of Jewish teaching, and it uses a wrestling match too. So who wins when strength shows up heavy?

teach.b: The book is the Tanya, by the Chabad teacher Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi. In chapter twenty-six he sets up the same match. Two people wrestle.
One is lazy and sluggish, and he'll be thrown easily, even if he's the stronger one. So it is, he says, with the struggle inside a person against the pull toward wrong. You can't win it heavy.
The heaviness he means comes from sadness, the flat, low kind that makes everything feel pointless. What wins is quickness, and quickness comes from joy. That's the surprise.

teach.h: JOY IS THE GRIP, NOT THE PRIZE.
teach.b: Joy isn't the prize at the end of the struggle. It's the grip you need to start it. The Psalms have the old line for it: Serve the LORD with gladness.
The Tanya isn't asking anyone to fake a smile, and it isn't waving away real grief.
Regret has its place, it says, at its own set time, the way you'd plan a hard conversation instead of having it all day long. What it warns against is letting the low mood run the whole match.
Its word for that mood is atzvut, a heavy sadness. And the opposite, simchah, joy, is more than a feeling here. It's a way of moving: lighter on your feet, first to the next move.
Back to the gym. The smaller kid isn't winning because nothing's hard.
He's winning because he came to wrestle glad.

how: The Tanya is a central text of Chabad Hasidism, studied in classes and in a daily study cycle; its call to serve God with joy rather than heaviness is a frequent theme at Hasidic gatherings, where songs are sung to lift the mood.

o: a sport where faith is said to decide who wins the match
the long night when Jacob fought an angel by the river
gladness as the strength to meet an inner struggle quickly

games.q: inside the match — tap the pairs.
p: has its place, at its own set time

s: joy is the reward you get after you win the struggle
in the Tanya it's the grip you need to start: joy brings the quickness that wins.
in the Tanya's picture, the stronger wrestler can still lose
if he's lazy and sluggish, he's thrown easily.
the Tanya says a person should never feel sorry about anything

games.q: your study group is way behind before finals and the mood keeps sinking. you're leading tonight. what would the Tanya's wrestler try first?
o: lift the room first, with something light, then move fast together.
list everything that's gone wrong, so everyone feels how serious it is.
call off tonight and wait until everyone actually feels ready to work.
games.why: in Tanya 26 heaviness makes even the stronger wrestler slow. joy isn't a reward for later; it's what gets you to the next move.

practice: Stand up if you can, or sit tall where you are. Shake out your hands, then your shoulders, for a few seconds, the way a wrestler loosens up before stepping onto the mat, then let yourself go still with your feet planted.
Bring to mind one thing you've been dragging your feet on, and see yourself taking the first step toward it lightly, quick and glad.

wordCard.voice: Joy to wrestle: the Tanya's picture of the inner struggle. Sadness makes a person sluggish; joy makes them quick enough to win.

orig.note: Hebrew: joy, gladness; in the Tanya, the lightness that makes a person quick in the inner struggle.

carryVoice: For the road: joy to wrestle, because heavy loses the match and glad gets the first move. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Tanya, Likutei Amarim, chapter 26 (two wrestlers: the lazy and sluggish one is easily thrown even if stronger; so too sadness and heaviness hinder the struggle with the evil inclination; joy brings alacrity)
